Analyzers.Title: "string.Create" should be used instead of "FormattableString"
Analyzers.Description: In order to produce a formatted string, both string.Create and either FormattableString.Invariant or FormattableString.CurrentCulture can be used. However, string.Create rents array buffers from ArrayPool<char> making it more performant, as well as preventing unnecessary allocations and future stress on the Garbage Collector.

Analyzers.Title: Using unsafe code blocks is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Using unsafe code blocks can lead to unintended security or stability risks.

Analyzers.Title: The code block contains too many logging calls
Analyzers.Description: A code block should not contain too many logging statements of a specific level.

Analyzers.Title: Logging in a catch clause should pass the caught exception as a parameter.
Analyzers.Description: This rule raises an issue on logging calls inside a catch clause that does not pass the raised Exception.

Analyzers.Title: Logging arguments should be passed to the correct parameter
Analyzers.Description: Most logging frameworks have methods that take a log level, an event ID or an exception as a separate input next to the log format and its arguments. There is a high chance that if the log level, the event ID or the exception are passed as the arguments to the message format, it was a mistake. This rule is going to raise in that scenario.

Analyzers.Title: Logger field or property name should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Sharing some naming conventions is a key point to make it possible for a team to efficiently collaborate. This rule checks that the logger field or property name matches a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: "Trace.Write" and "Trace.WriteLine" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Trace.Write and Trace.WriteLine methods are writing to the underlying output stream directly, bypassing the trace formatting and filtering performed by TraceListener.TraceEvent implementations. It is preferred to use Trace.TraceError, Trace.TraceWarning, and Trace.TraceInformation methods instead because they call the TraceEvent method which filters the trace output according to the TraceEventType (Error, Warning or Information) and enhance the output with additional information.

Analyzers.Title: Generic logger injection should match enclosing type
Analyzers.Description: In most logging frameworks, it’s good practice to set the logger name to match its enclosing type, as enforced by {rule:csharpsquid:S3416}.

Analyzers.Title: Log message template placeholders should be in the right order
Analyzers.Description: The positions of arguments in a logging call should match the positions of their message template placeholders.

Analyzers.Title: Log message template should be syntactically correct
Analyzers.Description: A message template must conform to the specification. The rule raises an issue if the template string violates the template string grammar.

Analyzers.Title: "Trace.WriteLineIf" should not be used with "TraceSwitch" levels
Analyzers.Description: The Trace.WriteLineIf Method from the System.Diagnostic.Trace facility writes a trace if the condition passed as the first parameter is true.

Analyzers.Title: Message template placeholders should be unique
Analyzers.Description: Named placeholders in message templates should be unique. The meaning of the named placeholders is to store the value of the provided argument under that name, enabling easier log querying. Since the named placeholder is used multiple times, it cannot store the different values uniquely with each name hence not serving its original purpose. There can be different behaviours when using the same named placeholder multiple times:

Analyzers.Title: Use PascalCase for named placeholders
Analyzers.Description: Within a message template each named placeholder should be in PascalCase.

Analyzers.Title: Blazor query parameter type should be supported
Analyzers.Description: The SupplyParameterFromQuery attribute can be used to specify that a component parameter, of a routable component, comes from the query string.

Analyzers.Title: [JSInvokable] attribute should only be used on public methods
Analyzers.Description: In Blazor, the [JSInvokable] attribute is used to annotate a method, enabling it to be invoked from JavaScript code. The prerequisite for this functionality is that the method must be declared as public. Otherwise, a runtime error will be triggered when an attempt is made to call the method from JavaScript.

Analyzers.Title: Component parameter type should match the route parameter type constraint
Analyzers.Description: In Blazor, when a route parameter constraint is applied, the value is automatically cast to the corresponding component parameter type. If the constraint type does not match the component parameter type, it can lead to confusion and potential runtime errors due to unsuccessful casting. Therefore, it is crucial to ensure that the types of route parameters and component parameters match to prevent such issues and maintain code clarity.

Analyzers.Title: Using lambda expressions in loops should be avoided in Blazor markup section
Analyzers.Description: In Blazor, using lambda expressions as event handlers when the UI elements are rendered in a loop can lead to negative user experiences and performance issues. This is particularly noticeable when rendering a large number of elements.

Analyzers.Title: Parameters with SupplyParameterFromQuery attribute should be used only in routable components
Analyzers.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

Analyzers.Title: Backslash should be avoided in route templates
Analyzers.Description: Backslash characters (\) should be avoided in route templates.

Analyzers.Title: ASP.NET controller actions should not have a route template starting with "/"
Analyzers.Description: Route templates for ASP.NET controller actions, defined via a RouteAttribute or any derivation of HttpMethodAttribute, should not start with "/".

Analyzers.Title: Use model binding instead of reading raw request data
Analyzers.Description: The HttpRequest class provides access to the raw request data through the QueryString, Headers, and Forms properties. However, whenever possible it is recommended to use model binding instead of directly accessing the input data.

Analyzers.Title: A Route attribute should be added to the controller when a route template is specified at the action level
Analyzers.Description: When a route template is defined through an attribute on an action method, conventional routing for that action is disabled. To maintain good practice, it’s recommended not to combine conventional and attribute-based routing within a single controller to avoid unpredicted behavior. As such, the controller should exclude itself from conventional routing by applying a [Route] attribute.

Analyzers.Title: Controllers should not have mixed responsibilities
Analyzers.Description: ASP.NET controllers should not have mixed responsibilities. Following the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP), they should be kept lean and focused on a single, separate concern. In short, they should have a single reason to change.

Analyzers.Title: API Controllers should derive from ControllerBase instead of Controller
Analyzers.Description: In ASP.NET Core, controllers usually inherit either from ControllerBase or Controller. If a controller does not use any View-specific functionality, it is recommended to inherit from ControllerBase.

Analyzers.Title: You should pool HTTP connections with HttpClientFactory
Analyzers.Description: In frequently used code paths, such as controller actions, you should avoid using the HttpClient directly and opt for one of the IHttpClientFactory-based mechanisms instead. This way, you avoid wasting resources and creating performance overhead.

Analyzers.Title: Value type property used as input in a controller action should be nullable, required or annotated with the JsonRequiredAttribute to avoid under-posting.
Analyzers.Description: "Under-posting" refers to a situation where a client sends less data than expected to the server during an HTTP request, for example when the client omits some properties from the request body that the server expects to receive.

Analyzers.Title: REST API actions should be annotated with an HTTP verb attribute
Analyzers.Description: When building a REST API, it’s recommended to annotate the controller actions with the available HTTP attributes to be precise about what your API supports.

Analyzers.Title: Awaitable method should be used
Analyzers.Description: In an async method, any blocking operations should be avoided.

Analyzers.Title: ModelState.IsValid should be called in controller actions
Analyzers.Description: In the context of ASP.NET Core MVC web applications, both model binding and model validation are processes that take place prior to the execution of a controller action. It is imperative for the application to examine the ModelState.IsValid and respond accordingly.

Analyzers.Title: Actions that return a value should be annotated with ProducesResponseTypeAttribute containing the return type
Analyzers.Description: In an ASP.NET Core Web API, controller actions can optionally return a result value. If a controller action returns a value in the happy path, for example ControllerBase.Ok(Object), annotating the action with one of the [ProducesResponseType] overloads that describe the type is recommended.

Analyzers.Title: Content Security Policies should be restrictive
Analyzers.Description: The Content Security Policy (CSP) is a computer security standard that serves as an additional layer of protection against various types of attacks, including Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and clickjacking. It provides a set of standard procedures for loading resources by user agents, which can help to mitigate the risk of content injection vulnerabilities.

Class names should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently.

Analyzers.Title: Lines should not be too long
Analyzers.Description: Scrolling horizontally to see a full line of code lowers the code readability.

Analyzers.Title: Files should not have too many lines of code
Analyzers.Description: When a source file grows too much, it can accumulate numerous responsibilities and become challenging to understand and maintain.

Analyzers.Title: Tabulation characters should not be used
Analyzers.Description: The tab width can differ from one development environment to another. Using tabs may require other developers to configure their environment (text editor, preferences, etc.) to read source code.

Analyzers.Title: Procedures should not have too many parameters
Analyzers.Description: Procedures with a long parameter list are difficult to use because maintainers must figure out the role of each parameter and keep track of their position.

Analyzers.Title: Nested blocks of code should not be left empty
Analyzers.Description: An empty code block is confusing. It will require some effort from maintainers to determine if it is intentional or indicates the implementation is incomplete.

Analyzers.Title: General or reserved exceptions should never be thrown
Analyzers.Description: This rule raises an issue when a generic exception (such as Exception, SystemException, ApplicationException, IndexOutOfRangeException, NullReferenceException, OutOfMemoryException or ExecutionEngineException) is thrown.

Analyzers.Title: Interface names should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Sharing some naming conventions is a key point to make it possible for a team to efficiently collaborate.

Analyzers.Title: Local variable names should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Local variables should be named consistently to communicate intent and improve maintainability. Rename your local variable to follow your project’s naming convention to address this issue.

Analyzers.Title: Generic type parameter names should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Inconsistent naming conventions can lead to confusion and errors when working in a team. This rule ensures that all generic type parameter names follow a consistent naming convention by checking them against a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Statements should be on separate lines
Analyzers.Description: Putting multiple statements on a single line lowers the code readability and makes debugging the code more complex.

Analyzers.Title: "If ... ElseIf" constructs should end with "Else" clauses
Analyzers.Description: This rule applies whenever an If statement is followed by one or more ElseIf statements; the final ElseIf should be followed by an Else statement.

Analyzers.Title: "Select" statements should end with a "Case Else" clause
Analyzers.Description: The requirement for a final Case Else clause is defensive programming.

Analyzers.Title: Control flow statements "If", "For", "For Each", "Do", "While", "Select" and "Try" should not be nested too deeply
Analyzers.Description: Nested control flow statements If, Select, For, For Each, While, Do, and Try are often key ingredients in creating what’s known as "Spaghetti code". This code smell can make your program difficult to understand and maintain.

Analyzers.Title: Procedures should not have too many lines of code
Analyzers.Description: A procedure that grows too large tends to aggregate too many responsibilities.

Analyzers.Title: Comments should not be located at the end of lines of code
Analyzers.Description: This rule verifies that single-line comments are not located at the ends of lines of code. The main idea behind this rule is that in order to be really readable, trailing comments would have to be properly written and formatted (correct alignment, no interference with the visual structure of the code, not too long to be visible) but most often, automatic code formatters would not handle this correctly: the code would end up less readable. Comments are far better placed on the previous empty line of code, where they will always be visible and properly formatted.

Analyzers.Title: "GoTo" statements should not be used
Analyzers.Description: GoTo is an unstructured control flow statement. It makes code less readable and maintainable. Structured control flow statements such as If, For, While, or Exit should be used instead.

Analyzers.Title: Parameter names should match base declaration
Analyzers.Description: Parameters are part of the method signature and its identity.

Analyzers.Title: Finalize method should not throw exceptions
Analyzers.Description: The Finalize methods are used to perform any necessary final clean-up when the garbage collector is collecting a class instance. The programmer has no control over when the Finalize method is called; the garbage collector decides when to call it.

Analyzers.Title: Mergeable "if" statements should be combined
Analyzers.Description: Nested code - blocks of code inside blocks of code - is eventually necessary, but increases complexity. This is why keeping the code as flat as possible, by avoiding unnecessary nesting, is considered a good practice.

Analyzers.Title: Expressions should not be too complex
Analyzers.Description: Complex boolean expressions are hard to read and so to maintain.

Analyzers.Title: URIs should not be hardcoded
Analyzers.Description: Hard-coding a URI makes it difficult to test a program for a variety of reasons:

Analyzers.Title: Redundant pairs of parentheses should be removed
Analyzers.Description: The use of parentheses, even those not required to enforce a desired order of operations, can clarify the intent behind a piece of code. However, redundant pairs of parentheses could be misleading and should be removed.

Analyzers.Title: "Obsolete" attributes should include explanations
Analyzers.Description: The Obsolete attribute can be applied with or without a message argument. Marking something Obsolete without including advice on why it’s obsolete or what to use instead will lead maintainers to waste time trying to figure those things out.

Analyzers.Title: Boolean literals should not be redundant
Analyzers.Description: A boolean literal can be represented in two different ways: True or False. They can be combined with logical operators (Not, And, Or, =) to produce logical expressions that represent truth values. However, comparing a boolean literal to a variable or expression that evaluates to a boolean value is unnecessary and can make the code harder to read and understand. The more complex a boolean expression is, the harder it will be for developers to understand its meaning and expected behavior, and it will favour the introduction of new bugs.

Analyzers.Title: Deprecated code should be removed
Analyzers.Description: This rule is meant to be used as a way to track code which is marked as being deprecated. Deprecated code should eventually be removed.

Analyzers.Title: Track uses of "FIXME" tags
Analyzers.Description: FIXME tags are commonly used to mark places where a bug is suspected, but which the developer wants to deal with later.

Analyzers.Title: Track uses of "TODO" tags
Analyzers.Description: Developers often use TODO tags to mark areas in the code where additional work or improvements are needed but are not implemented immediately. However, these TODO tags sometimes get overlooked or forgotten, leading to incomplete or unfinished code. This rule aims to identify and address unattended TODO tags to ensure a clean and maintainable codebase. This description explores why this is a problem and how it can be fixed to improve the overall code quality.

Analyzers.Title: "End" statements should not be used
Analyzers.Description: End statements exit the control flow of the program in an unstructured way. This statement stops code execution immediately without executing Dispose or Finalize methods, or executing Finally blocks. Therefore, it should be avoided.

Analyzers.Title: "Select...Case" clauses should not have too many lines of code
Analyzers.Description: The Select...Case statement should be used only to clearly define some new branches in the control flow. As soon as a case clause contains too many statements this highly decreases the readability of the overall control flow statement. In such case, the content of the case clause should be extracted into a dedicated procedure.

Analyzers.Title: "Any()" should be used to test for emptiness
Analyzers.Description: Using .Count() to test for emptiness works, but using .Any() makes the intent clearer, and the code more readable. However, there are some cases where special attention should be paid:

Analyzers.Title: Exceptions should not be thrown in finally blocks
Analyzers.Description: If an exception is already being thrown within the try block or caught in a catch block, throwing another exception in the finally block will override the original exception. This means that the original exception’s message and stack trace will be lost, potentially making it challenging to diagnose and troubleshoot the root cause of the problem.

Analyzers.Title: Unused procedure parameters should be removed
Analyzers.Description: A typical code smell known as unused function parameters refers to parameters declared in a function but not used anywhere within the function’s body. While this might seem harmless at first glance, it can lead to confusion and potential errors in your code. Disregarding the values passed to such parameters, the function’s behavior will be the same, but the programmer’s intention won’t be clearly expressed anymore. Therefore, removing function parameters that are not being utilized is considered best practice.

Analyzers.Title: Methods should not be empty
Analyzers.Description: An empty method is generally considered bad practice and can lead to confusion, readability, and maintenance issues. Empty methods bring no functionality and are misleading to others as they might think the method implementation fulfills a specific and identified requirement.

Analyzers.Title: String literals should not be duplicated
Analyzers.Description: Duplicated string literals make the process of refactoring complex and error-prone, as any change would need to be propagated on all occurrences.

Analyzers.Title: Array designators "()" should be on the type, not the variable
Analyzers.Description: Array designators should always be located on the type for better code readability. Otherwise, developers must look both at the type and the variable name to know whether or not a variable is an array.

Analyzers.Title: Method parameters and caught exceptions should not be reassigned
Analyzers.Description: While it is technically correct to assign to parameters from within method bodies, doing so before the parameter value is read is likely a bug. Instead, initial values of parameters should be, if not treated as readonly then at least read before reassignment.

Analyzers.Title: "Select" statements should have at least 3 "Case" clauses
Analyzers.Description: switch statements are useful when there are many different cases depending on the value of the same expression.

Analyzers.Title: Using hardcoded IP addresses is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Hardcoding IP addresses is security-sensitive. It has led in the past to the following vulnerabilities:

Analyzers.Title: Track lack of copyright and license headers
Analyzers.Description: Each source file should start with a header stating file ownership and the license which must be used to distribute the application.

Analyzers.Title: "Select Case" statement with many "Case" clauses should have only one statement
Analyzers.Description: When Select Case statements have large sets of multi-line Case clauses, the code becomes hard to read and maintain.

Analyzers.Title: Unused local variables should be removed
Analyzers.Description: An unused local variable is a variable that has been declared but is not used anywhere in the block of code where it is defined. It is dead code, contributing to unnecessary complexity and leading to confusion when reading the code. Therefore, it should be removed from your code to maintain clarity and efficiency.

Analyzers.Title: Functions, procedures and properties should not be too complex
Analyzers.Description: The cyclomatic complexity of a function, procedure or property should not exceed a defined threshold. Complex code can perform poorly and will in any case be difficult to understand and therefore to maintain.

Analyzers.Title: Functions and procedures should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all subroutine and function names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Strings should not be concatenated using "+" or "&" in a loop
Analyzers.Description: StringBuilder is more efficient than string concatenation, especially when the operator is repeated over and over as in loops.

Analyzers.Title: The "&" operator should be used to concatenate strings
Analyzers.Description: Consistently using the & operator for string concatenation make the developer intentions clear.

Analyzers.Title: Method parameters should follow a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Sharing some naming conventions is a key point to make it possible for a team to efficiently collaborate.

Analyzers.Title: Variables should not be self-assigned
Analyzers.Description: There is no reason to re-assign a variable to itself. Either this statement is redundant and should be removed, or the re-assignment is a mistake and some other value or variable was intended for the assignment instead.

Analyzers.Title: Multiple variables should not be declared on the same line
Analyzers.Description: Declaring multiple variable on one line is difficult to read.

Analyzers.Title: Loops with at most one iteration should be refactored
Analyzers.Description: A loop statement with at most one iteration is equivalent to an If statement; the following block is executed only once.

Analyzers.Title: Identical expressions should not be used on both sides of a binary operator
Analyzers.Description: Using the same value on either side of a binary operator is almost always a mistake. In the case of logical operators, it is either a copy/paste error and therefore a bug, or it is simply wasted code, and should be simplified. In the case of most binary mathematical operators, having the same value on both sides of an operator yields predictable results, and should be simplified.

Analyzers.Title: "Select Case" statements should not be nested
Analyzers.Description: Nested Select Case structures are difficult to understand because you can easily confuse the cases of an inner Select Case as belonging to an outer statement. Therefore nested Select Case statements should be avoided.

Analyzers.Title: Related "If/ElseIf" statements should not have the same condition
Analyzers.Description: A chain of If/ElseIf statements is evaluated from top to bottom. At most, only one branch will be executed: the first statement with a condition that evaluates to True. Therefore, duplicating a condition leads to unreachable code inside the duplicated condition block. Usually, this is due to a copy/paste error.

Analyzers.Title: Two branches in a conditional structure should not have exactly the same implementation
Analyzers.Description: When the same code is duplicated in two or more separate branches of a conditional, it can make the code harder to understand, maintain, and can potentially introduce bugs if one instance of the code is changed but others are not.

Analyzers.Title: Boolean checks should not be inverted
Analyzers.Description: It is needlessly complex to invert the result of a boolean comparison. The opposite comparison should be made instead.

Analyzers.Title: Invalid casts should be avoided
Analyzers.Description: A cast is an explicit conversion, which is a way to tell the compiler the intent to convert from one type to another.

Analyzers.Title: Hard-coded credentials are security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Because it is easy to extract strings from an application source code or binary, credentials should not be hard-coded. This is particularly true for applications that are distributed or that are open-source.

Analyzers.Title: Formatting SQL queries is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Formatted SQL queries can be difficult to maintain, debug and can increase the risk of SQL injection when concatenating untrusted values into the query. However, this rule doesn’t detect SQL injections, the goal is only to highlight complex/formatted queries.

Analyzers.Title: Classes should not be empty
Analyzers.Description: There is no good excuse for an empty class. If it’s being used simply as a common extension point, it should be replaced with an interface. If it was stubbed in as a placeholder for future development it should be fleshed-out. In any other case, it should be eliminated.

Analyzers.Title: Classes named like "Exception" should extend "Exception" or a subclass
Analyzers.Description: Clear, communicative naming is important in code. It helps maintainers and API users understand the intentions for and uses of a unit of code. Using "exception" in the name of a class that does not extend Exception or one of its subclasses is a clear violation of the expectation that a class' name will indicate what it is and/or does.

Analyzers.Title: Short-circuit logic should be used in boolean contexts
Analyzers.Description: Short-circuit evaluation is an evaluation strategy for Boolean operators, that doesn’t evaluate the second argument of the operator if it is not needed to determine the result of the operation.

Analyzers.Title: "ToString()" method should not return Nothing
Analyzers.Description: Calling ToString() on an object should always return a string. Thus, overriding the ToString method should never return Nothing because it breaks the method’s implicit contract, and as a result the consumer’s expectations.

Analyzers.Title: Arguments should be passed in the same order as the procedure parameters
Analyzers.Description: Calling a procedure with argument variables whose names match the procedure parameter names but in a different order can cause confusion. It could indicate a mistake in the arguments' order, leading to unexpected results.

Analyzers.Title: Using non-standard cryptographic algorithms is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: The use of a non-standard algorithm is dangerous because a determined attacker may be able to break the algorithm and compromise whatever data has been protected. Standard algorithms like AES, RSA, SHA, …​ should be used instead.

Analyzers.Title: "NameOf" should be used
Analyzers.Description: Because parameter names could be changed during refactoring, they should not be spelled out literally in strings. Instead, use NameOf(), and the string that’s output will always be correct.

Analyzers.Title: Namespace names should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all namespace names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Public constant members should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Constant members are copied at compile time to the call sites, instead of being fetched at runtime.

Analyzers.Title: "Do" loops should not be used without a "While" or "Until" condition
Analyzers.Description: A Do ... Loop without a While or Until condition must be terminated by an unstructured Exit Do statement. It is safer and more readable to use structured loops instead.

Analyzers.Title: Enumeration types should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all enum names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Enumeration values should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all enumeration value names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Enumeration type names should not have "Flags" or "Enum" suffixes
Analyzers.Description: The information that an enumeration type is actually an enumeration or a set of flags should not be duplicated in its name.

Analyzers.Title: Flags enumerations should explicitly initialize all their members
Analyzers.Description: When you annotate an Enum with the Flags attribute, you must not rely on the values that are automatically set by the language to the Enum members, but you should define the enumeration constants in powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, and so on). Automatic value initialization will set the first member to zero and increment the value by one for each subsequent member. As a result, you won’t be able to use the enum members with bitwise operators.

Analyzers.Title: Flags enumerations zero-value members should be named "None"
Analyzers.Description: An enumeration can be decorated with the FlagsAttribute to indicate that it can be used as a bit field: a set of flags, that can be independently set and reset.

Analyzers.Title: Event handlers should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all even handler names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Events should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all even names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Event names should not have "Before" or "After" as a prefix or suffix
Analyzers.Description: "After" and "Before" prefixes or suffixes should not be used to indicate pre and post events. The concepts of before and after should be given to events using the present and past tense.

Analyzers.Title: Indexed properties with more than one parameter should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Indexed properties are meant to represent access to a logical collection. When multiple parameters are required, this design guideline may be violated, and refactoring the property into a method is preferable.

Analyzers.Title: Line continuations should not be used
Analyzers.Description: To improve the code readability, the explicit line continuation character, _, should not be used. Instead, it is better to break lines after an operator.

Analyzers.Title: Array literals should be used instead of array creation expressions
Analyzers.Description: Array literals are more compact than array creation expressions.

Analyzers.Title: Fields should be private
Analyzers.Description: Fields should not be part of an API, and therefore should always be private. Indeed, they cannot be added to an interface for instance, and validation cannot be added later on without breaking backward compatibility. Instead, developers should encapsulate their fields into properties. Explicit property getters and setters can be introduced for validation purposes or to smooth the transition to a newer system.

Analyzers.Title: "IsNot" should be used instead of "Not ... Is ..."
Analyzers.Description: The ... IsNot ... syntax is more compact and more readable than the Not ... Is ... syntax.

Analyzers.Title: "On Error" statements should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Prefer the use of Try ... Catch blocks instead of On Error statements.

Analyzers.Title: Optional parameters should not be used
Analyzers.Description: The overloading mechanism should be used in place of optional parameters for several reasons:

Analyzers.Title: Private constants should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all Private Const field names comply with the provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: "Private Shared ReadOnly" fields should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all Private Shared ReadOnly field names comply with the provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: "Private" fields should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all Private field names match the provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Properties should not make collection or array copies
Analyzers.Description: Most developers expect property access to be as efficient as field access. However, if a property returns a copy of an array or collection, it will be much slower than a simple field access, contrary to the caller’s likely expectations. Therefore, such properties should be refactored into methods so that callers are not surprised by the unexpectedly poor performance.

Analyzers.Title: Properties should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that property names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Non-private constants should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private Const field names comply with the provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Public methods should not have multidimensional array parameters
Analyzers.Description: Using multidimensional and jagged arrays as method parameters in C# can be challenging for developers.

Analyzers.Title: Non-private fields should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared coding conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private fields names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Non-private "Shared ReadOnly" fields should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: Shared naming conventions allow teams to collaborate efficiently. This rule checks that all non-private Shared ReadOnly fields names match a provided regular expression.

Analyzers.Title: Exceptions should not be thrown from property getters
Analyzers.Description: Property getters should be simple operations that are always safe to call. If exceptions need to be thrown, it is best to convert the property to a method.

Analyzers.Title: Generic type parameter names should comply with a naming convention
Analyzers.Description: This rule is deprecated; use {rule:vbnet:S119} instead.

Analyzers.Title: Signed types should be preferred to unsigned ones
Analyzers.Description: Unsigned integers have different arithmetic operators than signed ones - operators that few developers understand. Therefore, signed types should be preferred where possible.

Analyzers.Title: "With" statements should be used for a series of calls to the same object
Analyzers.Description: Using the With statement for a series of calls to the same object makes the code more readable.

Analyzers.Title: Write-only properties should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Properties with only setters are confusing and counterintuitive. Instead, a property getter should be added if possible, or the property should be replaced with a setter method.

Analyzers.Title: Child class fields should not shadow parent class fields
Analyzers.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

Analyzers.Title: Arrays should be initialized using the "... = {}" syntax
Analyzers.Description: The ... = {} syntax is more compact, more readable and less error-prone.

Analyzers.Title: Unnecessary bit operations should not be performed
Analyzers.Description: Certain bitwise operations are not needed and should not be performed because their results are predictable.

Analyzers.Title: Shared resources should not be used for locking
Analyzers.Description: The instance passed to the SyncLock statement should be a dedicated private field.

Analyzers.Title: Setting loose POSIX file permissions is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: In Unix, "others" class refers to all users except the owner of the file and the members of the group assigned to this file.

Analyzers.Title: "IndexOf" checks should not be for positive numbers
Analyzers.Description: Most checks against an IndexOf value compare it with -1 because 0 is a valid index.

Analyzers.Title: "catch" clauses should do more than rethrow
Analyzers.Description: A Catch clause that only rethrows the caught exception has the same effect as omitting the Catch altogether and letting it bubble up automatically.

Analyzers.Title: Non-existent operators like "=+" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Using operator pairs (=+ or =-) that look like reversed single operators (+= or -=) is confusing. They compile and run but do not produce the same result as their mirrored counterpart.

Analyzers.Title: 'Not' boolean operator should not be repeated
Analyzers.Description: The repetition of the Not operator is usually a typo. The second operator invalidates the first one:

Analyzers.Title: "Thread.Sleep" should not be used in tests
Analyzers.Description: Using Thread.Sleep in a test might introduce unpredictable and inconsistent results depending on the environment. Furthermore, it will block the thread, which means the system resources are not being fully used.

Analyzers.Title: "Exit Select" statements should not be used redundantly
Analyzers.Description: Visual Basic .NET, unlike many other programming languages, has no "fall-through" for its Select cases. Each case already has an implicit Exit Select as its last instruction. It therefore is redundant to explicitly add one.

Analyzers.Title: Reflection should not be used to increase accessibility of classes, methods, or fields
Analyzers.Description: Altering or bypassing the accessibility of classes, methods, or fields through reflection violates the encapsulation principle. This can break the internal contracts of the accessed target and lead to maintainability issues and runtime errors.

Analyzers.Title: "StringBuilder" data should be used
Analyzers.Description: StringBuilder instances that never build a string clutter the code and worse are a drag on performance. Either they should be removed, or the missing ToString() call should be added.

Analyzers.Title: If operators should not be nested
Analyzers.Description: Nested ternaries are hard to read and can make the order of operations complex to understand.

Analyzers.Title: Date and time should not be used as a type for primary keys
Analyzers.Description: You should only set a property of a temporal type (like DateTime or DateTimeOffset) as the primary key of a table if the values are guaranteed to be unique.

Analyzers.Title: "Exit" statements should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Exit Function, Exit Property, and Exit Sub are all poor, less-readable substitutes for a simple Return, and if used with code that should return a value (Exit Function and in some cases Exit Property) they could result in a NullReferenceException.

Analyzers.Title: "[ExpectedException]" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: It should be clear to a casual reader what code a test is testing and what results are expected. Unfortunately, that’s not usually the case with the ExpectedException attribute since an exception could be thrown from almost any line in the method.

Analyzers.Title: Right operands of shift operators should be integers
Analyzers.Description: Numbers can be shifted with the << and >> operators, but the right operand of the operation needs to be an int or a type that has an implicit conversion to int. However, when the left operand is an object, the compiler’s type checking is turned off, therfore you can pass anything to the right of a shift operator and have it compile. If the argument can’t be implicitly converted to int at runtime, a RuntimeBinderException will be raised.

Analyzers.Title: Classes should not have only "private" constructors
Analyzers.Description: When a class has only a private constructor, it can’t be instantiated except within the class itself. Such classes can be considered dead code and should be fixed

Analyzers.Title: Type inheritance should not be recursive
Analyzers.Description: Recursion is a technique used to define a problem in terms of the problem itself, usually in terms of a simpler version of the problem itself.

Analyzers.Title: Optional parameters should be passed to "base" calls
Analyzers.Description: When optional parameter values are not passed to base method calls, the value passed in by the caller is ignored. This can cause the function to behave differently than expected, leading to errors and making the code difficult to debug.

Analyzers.Title: One-way "OperationContract" methods should have "void" return type
Analyzers.Description: When declaring a Windows Communication Foundation (WCF) OperationContract method as one-way, that service method won’t return any result, not even an underlying empty confirmation message. These are fire-and-forget methods that are useful in event-like communication. Therefore, specifying a return type has no effect and can confuse readers.

Analyzers.Title: Methods with "Pure" attribute should return a value
Analyzers.Description: Marking a method with the Pure attribute indicates that the method doesn’t make any visible state changes. Therefore, a Pure method should return a result. Otherwise, it indicates a no-operation call.

Analyzers.Title: Cognitive Complexity of methods should not be too high
Analyzers.Description: This rule raises an issue when the code cognitive complexity of a function is above a certain threshold.

Analyzers.Title: "ByVal" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Since Visual Studio 2010 SP1, the ByVal parameter modifier is implicitly applied, and therefore not required anymore. Removing it from your source code will improve readability.

Analyzers.Title: "IIf" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Visual Basic .NET offers a non-short-circuit conditional function, IIf(), which returns either its second or third parameter based on the expression in the first parameter. Using it is slower than using If() because each parameter is unconditionally evaluated. Further, its use can lead to runtime exceptions because IIf always evaluates all three of its arguments.

Analyzers.Title: "SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle" should not be called
Analyzers.Description: The SafeHandle.DangerousGetHandle method poses significant risks and should be used carefully. This method carries the inherent danger of potentially returning an invalid handle, which can result in resource leaks and security vulnerabilities. Although it is technically possible to utilize this method without encountering issues, doing so correctly requires a high level of expertise. Therefore, it is recommended to avoid using this method altogether.

Analyzers.Title: Exception types should be "Public"
Analyzers.Description: The point of having custom exception types is to convey more information than is available in standard types. But custom exception types must be public for that to work.

Analyzers.Title: Arrays should not be created for ParamArray parameters
Analyzers.Description: There’s no point in creating an array solely for the purpose of passing it to a ParamArray parameter. Simply pass the elements directly. They will be consolidated into an array automatically.

Analyzers.Title: "CoSetProxyBlanket" and "CoInitializeSecurity" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

Analyzers.Title: "Thread.Resume" and "Thread.Suspend" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Thread.Suspend and Thread.Resume can give unpredictable results, and both methods have been deprecated. Indeed, if Thread.Suspend is not used very carefully, a thread can be suspended while holding a lock, thus leading to a deadlock.

Analyzers.Title: Value types should implement "IEquatable<T>"
Analyzers.Description: If you’re using a Structure, it is likely because you’re interested in performance. But by failing to implement IEquatable<T> you’re loosing performance when comparisons are made because without IEquatable<T>, boxing and reflection are used to make comparisons.

Analyzers.Title: Types should be defined in named namespaces
Analyzers.Description: Types are declared in namespaces in order to prevent name collisions and as a way to organize them into the object hierarchy. Types that are defined outside any named namespace are in a global namespace that cannot be referenced in code.

Analyzers.Title: Assemblies should have version information
Analyzers.Description: The AssemblyVersion attribute is used to specify the version number of an assembly. An assembly is a compiled unit of code, which can be marked with a version number by applying the attribute to an assembly’s source code file.

Analyzers.Title: All branches in a conditional structure should not have exactly the same implementation
Analyzers.Description: Having all branches of a Select Case or If chain with the same implementation indicates a problem.

Analyzers.Title: Deserialization methods should be provided for "OptionalField" members
Analyzers.Description: Fields marked with System.Runtime.Serialization.OptionalFieldAttribute are serialized just like any other field. But such fields are ignored on deserialization, and retain the default values associated with their types. Therefore, deserialization event handlers should be declared to set such fields during the deserialization process.

Analyzers.Title: Serialization event handlers should be implemented correctly
Analyzers.Description: Serialization event handlers that don’t have the correct signature will not be called, bypassing augmentations to automated serialization and deserialization events.

Analyzers.Title: Collection sizes and array length comparisons should make sense
Analyzers.Description: The size of a collection and the length of an array are always greater than or equal to zero. Testing it doesn’t make sense, since the result is always true.

Analyzers.Title: Assemblies should be marked as CLS compliant
Analyzers.Description: Assemblies should conform with the Common Language Specification (CLS) in order to be usable across programming languages. To be compliant an assembly has to indicate it with System.CLSCompliantAttribute.

Analyzers.Title: Assemblies should explicitly specify COM visibility
Analyzers.Description: Assemblies should explicitly indicate whether they are meant to be COM visible or not. If the ComVisibleAttribute is not present, the default is to make the content of the assembly visible to COM clients.

Analyzers.Title: Threads should not lock on objects with weak identity
Analyzers.Description: Objects that can be accessed across application domain boundaries are said to have weak identity. This means that these objects can be considered shared resources outside of the domain, which can be lead to them being accessed or modified by multiple threads or concurrent parts of a program, outside of the domain.

Analyzers.Title: Child class fields should not differ from parent class fields only by capitalization
Analyzers.Description: Having a field in a child class with a name that differs from a parent class' field only by capitalization is sure to cause confusion. Such child class fields should be renamed.

Analyzers.Title: Searching OS commands in PATH is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: When you run an OS command, it is always important to protect yourself against the risk of accidental or malicious replacement of the executables in the production system.

Analyzers.Title: Non-abstract attributes should be sealed
Analyzers.Description: The .NET framework class library provides methods for retrieving custom attributes. Sealing the attribute eliminates the search through the inheritance hierarchy, and can improve performance.

Analyzers.Title: Method overloads should be grouped together
Analyzers.Description: For clarity, all overloads of the same method should be grouped together. That lets both users and maintainers quickly understand all the current available options.

Analyzers.Title: Map values should not be replaced unconditionally
Analyzers.Description: Storing a value inside a collection at a given key or index and then unconditionally overwriting it without reading the initial value is a case of a "dead store".

Analyzers.Title: Methods should not have identical implementations
Analyzers.Description: Two methods having the same implementation are suspicious. It might be that something else was intended. Or the duplication is intentional, which becomes a maintenance burden.

Analyzers.Title: Classes should implement their "ExportAttribute" interfaces
Analyzers.Description: The Attributed Programming Model, also known as Attribute-oriented programming (@OP), is a programming model used to embed attributes within codes.

Analyzers.Title: Null checks should not be combined with "TypeOf Is" operator checks
Analyzers.Description: There’s no need to null test in conjunction with an TypeOf ... Is test. Nothing is not an instance of anything, so a null check is redundant.

Analyzers.Title: Windows Forms entry points should be marked with STAThread
Analyzers.Description: When an assembly uses Windows Forms (classes and interfaces from the System.Windows.Forms namespace) its entry point should be marked with the STAThreadAttribute to indicate that the threading model should be "Single-Threaded Apartment" (STA) which is the only one supported by Windows Forms.

Analyzers.Title: Extension methods should not extend "Object"
Analyzers.Description: Creating an extension method that extends Object is not recommended because it makes the method available on every type. Extensions should be applied at the most specialized level possible, and that is very unlikely to be Object.

Analyzers.Title: "ConstructorArgument" parameters should exist in constructors
Analyzers.Description: When creating a custom Markup Extension that accepts parameters in WPF, the ConstructorArgument markup must be used to identify the discrete properties that match these parameters. However since this is done via a string, the compiler won’t give you any warning in case there are typos.

Analyzers.Title: Property procedures should access the expected fields
Analyzers.Description: Properties provide a way to enforce encapsulation by providing property procedures that give controlled access to Private fields. However, in classes with multiple fields, it is not unusual that copy-and-paste is used to quickly create the needed properties, which can result in the wrong field being accessed by the property procedures.

Analyzers.Title: "Shared" parts should not be created with "new"
Analyzers.Description: Marking a class with PartCreationPolicy(CreationPolicy.Shared), which is part of Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), means that a single, shared instance of the exported object will be created. Therefore it doesn’t make sense to create new instances using the constructor and it will most likely result in unexpected behaviours.

Analyzers.Title: Weak SSL/TLS protocols should not be used
Analyzers.Description: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to a number of attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

Analyzers.Title: "PartCreationPolicyAttribute" should be used with "ExportAttribute"
Analyzers.Description: To customize the default behavior for an export in the Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), applying the PartCreationPolicyAttribute is necessary. For the PartCreationPolicyAttribute to be meaningful in the context of an export, the class must also be annotated with the ExportAttribute.

Analyzers.Title: Delivering code in production with debug features activated is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Development tools and frameworks usually have options to make debugging easier for developers. Although these features are useful during development, they should never be enabled for applications deployed in production. Debug instructions or error messages can leak detailed information about the system, like the application’s path or file names.

Analyzers.Title: "DebuggerDisplayAttribute" strings should reference existing members
Analyzers.Description: The DebuggerDisplayAttribute is used to determine how an object is displayed in the debugger window.

Analyzers.Title: "new Guid()" should not be used
Analyzers.Description: When the syntax new Guid() (i.e. parameterless instantiation) is used, it must be that one of three things is wanted:

Analyzers.Title: Calls to delegate's method "BeginInvoke" should be paired with calls to "EndInvoke"
Analyzers.Description: When calling the BeginInvoke method of a delegate, resources are allocated that are only freed up when EndInvoke is called. Failing to pair BeginInvoke with EndInvoke can lead to resource leaks and incomplete asynchronous calls.

Analyzers.Title: Non-async "Task/Task<T>" methods should not return null
Analyzers.Description: Returning Nothing from a non-Async Task/Task(Of TResult) procedure will cause a NullReferenceException at runtime if the procedure is awaited. This problem can be avoided by returning Task.CompletedTask or Task.FromResult(Of TResult)(Nothing) respectively.

Analyzers.Title: Comments should not be empty
Analyzers.Description: Empty comments, as shown in the example, hurt readability and might indicate an oversight.

Analyzers.Title: Using weak hashing algorithms is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Cryptographic hash algorithms such as MD2, MD4, MD5, MD6, HAVAL-128, DSA (which uses SHA-1), RIPEMD, RIPEMD-128, RIPEMD-160and SHA-1 are no longer considered secure, because it is possible to have collisions (little computational effort is enough to find two or more different inputs that produce the same hash).

Analyzers.Title: Configuring loggers is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: This rule is deprecated, and will eventually be removed.

Analyzers.Title: Server certificates should be verified during SSL/TLS connections
Analyzers.Description: This vulnerability makes it possible that an encrypted communication is intercepted.

Analyzers.Title: Expanding archive files without controlling resource consumption is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Successful Zip Bomb attacks occur when an application expands untrusted archive files without controlling the size of the expanded data, which can lead to denial of service. A Zip bomb is usually a malicious archive file of a few kilobytes of compressed data but turned into gigabytes of uncompressed data. To achieve this extreme compression ratio, attackers will compress irrelevant data (eg: a long string of repeated bytes).

Analyzers.Title: Using publicly writable directories is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Operating systems have global directories where any user has write access. Those folders are mostly used as temporary storage areas like /tmp in Linux based systems. An application manipulating files from these folders is exposed to race conditions on filenames: a malicious user can try to create a file with a predictable name before the application does. A successful attack can result in other files being accessed, modified, corrupted or deleted. This risk is even higher if the application runs with elevated permissions.

Analyzers.Title: Insecure temporary file creation methods should not be used
Analyzers.Description: Temporary files are considered insecurely created when the file existence check is performed separately from the actual file creation. Such a situation can occur when creating temporary files using normal file handling functions or when using dedicated temporary file handling functions that are not atomic.

Analyzers.Title: Encryption algorithms should be used with secure mode and padding scheme
Analyzers.Description: This vulnerability exposes encrypted data to a number of attacks whose goal is to recover the plaintext.

Analyzers.Title: Cipher algorithms should be robust
Analyzers.Description: This vulnerability makes it possible that the cleartext of the encrypted message might be recoverable without prior knowledge of the key.

Analyzers.Title: JWT should be signed and verified with strong cipher algorithms
Analyzers.Description: This vulnerability allows forging of JSON Web Tokens to impersonate other users.

Analyzers.Title: Allowing requests with excessive content length is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Rejecting requests with significant content length is a good practice to control the network traffic intensity and thus resource consumption in order to prevent DoS attacks.

Analyzers.Title: Disabling ASP.NET "Request Validation" feature is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: ASP.NET 1.1+ comes with a feature called Request Validation, preventing the server to accept content containing un-encoded HTML. This feature comes as a first protection layer against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks and act as a simple Web Application Firewall (WAF) rejecting requests potentially containing malicious content.

Analyzers.Title: Regular expressions should be syntactically valid
Analyzers.Description: Regular expressions have their own syntax that is understood by regular expression engines. Those engines will throw an exception at runtime if they are given a regular expression that does not conform to that syntax.

Analyzers.Title: "Return" statements should be used instead of assigning values to function names
Analyzers.Description: Functions can return values using two different syntaxes. The modern, and correct, way to do it is to use a Return statement. The VB6 way, i.e. old way, is to assign a return value to the function’s name .

Analyzers.Title: "Option Strict" should be enabled
Analyzers.Description: There are several compilations options available for Visual Basic source code and Option Strict defines compiler behavior for implicit data type conversions. Specifying Option Strict Off will allow:

Analyzers.Title: "Option Explicit" should be enabled
Analyzers.Description: There are several compilations options available for Visual Basic source code and Option Explicit defines compiler behavior for implicit variable declarations. Specifying Option Explicit Off will allow creating a variable by it’s first usage. This behavior can lead to unexpected runtime errors due to typos in variable names.

Analyzers.Title: Use a testable date/time provider
Analyzers.Description: One of the principles of a unit test is that it must have full control of the system under test. This is problematic when production code includes calls to static methods, which cannot be changed or controlled. Date/time functions are usually provided by system libraries as static methods.

Analyzers.Title: Hard-coded secrets are security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Because it is easy to extract strings from an application source code or binary, secrets should not be hard-coded. This is particularly true for applications that are distributed or that are open-source.

Analyzers.Title: Not specifying a timeout for regular expressions is security-sensitive
Analyzers.Description: Not specifying a timeout for regular expressions can lead to a Denial-of-Service attack. Pass a timeout when using System.Text.RegularExpressions to process untrusted input because a malicious user might craft a value for which the evaluation lasts excessively long.

Analyzers.Title: "ExcludeFromCodeCoverage" attributes should include a justification
Analyzers.Description: The ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is used to exclude portions of code from code coverage reporting. It is a bad practice to retain code that is not covered by unit tests. In .Net 5, the Justification property was added to the ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute as an opportunity to document the rationale for the exclusion. This rule raises an issue when no such justification is given.

Analyzers.Title: Avoid using "DateTime.Now" for benchmarking or timing operations
Analyzers.Description: The rule targets the use of DateTime.Now call followed by some arithmetic operation.

Analyzers.Title: Always set the "DateTimeKind" when creating new "DateTime" instances
Analyzers.Description: Not knowing the Kind of the DateTime object that an application is using can lead to misunderstandings when displaying or comparing them. Explicitly setting the Kind property helps the application to stay consistent, and its maintainers understand what kind of date is being managed. To achieve this, when instantiating a new DateTime object you should always use a constructor overload that allows you to define the Kind property.

Analyzers.Title: Use UTC when recording DateTime instants
Analyzers.Description: You should avoid recording time instants with the use of property DateTime.Now. The property DateTime.Now returns the current date and time expressed in the machine’s local time without containing any timezone-related information (for example, the offset from Coordinated Universal Time). Not having this information means that if you need to display this DateTime object or use it for computations in another machine placed in a different time zone, you won’t be able to reconstruct it in the second machine’s local time without knowing the origin’s offset. This will likely lead to confusion and potential bugs.

Analyzers.Title: Use "DateTimeOffset" instead of "DateTime"
Analyzers.Description: This rule recommends using DateTimeOffset instead of DateTime for projects targeting .NET Framework 2.0 or later.

Analyzers.Title: Use "TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById" without converting the timezones with "TimezoneConverter"
Analyzers.Description: Since .NET 6 you don’t have to use the TimeZoneConverter library to manually do the conversion between IANA and Windows timezones. The .NET 6.0 introduced new Time Zone enhancements, one being the TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById(string timezone) method now accepts as input both IANA and Windows time zone IDs on any operating system with installed time zone data. TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById will automatically convert its input from IANA to Windows and vice versa if the requested time zone is not found on the system.

Analyzers.Title: Use a format provider when parsing date and time
Analyzers.Description: When converting a string representation of a date and time to a DateTime object or any other temporal type with one of the available system parsing methods, you should always provide an IFormatProvider parameter.

Analyzers.Title: Don't hardcode the format when turning dates and times to strings
Analyzers.Description: Hardcoding the date and time format strings can lead to formats that consumers misunderstand. Also, if the same format is meant to be used in multiple places, it is easier to make a mistake when it’s hardcoded instead of using a format provided by an IFormatProvider or using one of the standard format strings.

Analyzers.Title: Use the "UnixEpoch" field instead of creating "DateTime" instances that point to the beginning of the Unix epoch
Analyzers.Description: With .NET Core the UnixEpoch field was introduced to DateTime and DateTimeOffset types. Using this field clearly states that the intention is to use the beginning of the Unix epoch.

Analyzers.Title: "Find" method should be used instead of the "FirstOrDefault" extension
Analyzers.Description: Both the List.Find method and the Enumerable.FirstOrDefault method can be used to locate the first element that meets a specified condition within a collection. However, for List objects, List.Find may offer superior performance compared to Enumerable.FirstOrDefault. While the performance difference might be negligible for small collections, it can become significant for larger collections. This observation also holds true for ImmutableList and arrays.

Analyzers.Title: The collection-specific "TrueForAll" method should be used instead of the "All" extension
Analyzers.Description: Both the List.TrueForAll method and the IEnumerable.All method can be used to check if all list elements satisfy a given condition in a collection. However, List.TrueForAll can be faster than IEnumerable.All for List objects. The performance difference may be minor for small collections, but for large collections, it can be noticeable.

Analyzers.Title: Collection-specific "Exists" method should be used instead of the "Any" extension
Analyzers.Description: Both the List.Exists method and IEnumerable.Any method can be used to find the first element that satisfies a predicate in a collection. However, List.Exists can be faster than IEnumerable.Any for List objects, as well as requires significantly less memory. For small collections, the performance difference may be negligible, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies to ImmutableList and arrays too.

Analyzers.Title: The collection should be filtered before sorting by using "Where" before "OrderBy"
Analyzers.Description: When working with LINQ in C#, it is recommended to pay attention to the order in which methods are chained, especially when using Where and OrderBy methods. It is advised to call the Where method before OrderBy because Where filters the elements of the sequence based on a given condition and returns a new sequence containing only the elements that satisfy that condition. Calling OrderBy before Where, may end up sorting elements that will be later discarded, which can lead to inefficiency. Conversely, calling Where before OrderBy, will first filter the sequence to include only the elements of interest, and then sort them based on the specified order.

Analyzers.Title: Prefer indexing instead of "Enumerable" methods on types implementing "IList"
Analyzers.Description: Indexes in C# provide direct access to an element at a specific position within an array or collection. When compared to Enumerable methods, indexing can be more efficient for certain scenarios, such as iterating over a large collection, due to avoiding the overhead of checking the underlying collection type before accessing it.

Analyzers.Title: "Min/Max" properties of "Set" types should be used instead of the "Enumerable" extension methods
Analyzers.Description: Both the Enumerable.Max extension method and the SortedSet<T>.Max property can be used to find the maximum value in a SortedSet<T>. However, SortedSet<T>.Max is much faster than Enumerable.Max. For small collections, the performance difference may be minor, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies for the Min property as well.

Analyzers.Title: "StartsWith" and "EndsWith" overloads that take a "char" should be used instead of the ones that take a "string"
Analyzers.Description: With string.StartsWith(char) and string.EndsWith(char), only the first character of the string is compared to the provided character, whereas the string versions of those methods have to do checks about the current StringComparison and CultureInfo. Thus, the char overloads are significantly faster for default comparison scenarios.

Analyzers.Title: The lambda parameter should be used instead of capturing arguments in "ConcurrentDictionary" methods
Analyzers.Description: When using the ConcurrentDictionary, there are many overloads of the GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate methods that take both a TKey argument and a lambda that expects a TKey parameter. This means that the right side of the lambda can be written using either the lambda’s parameter or the method’s argument. However, using the method’s argument leads to the lambda capturing it, and the compiler will need to generate a class and instantiate it before the call. This means memory allocations, as well as more time spend during Garbage Collection.

Analyzers.Title: "First" and "Last" properties of "LinkedList" should be used instead of the "First()" and "Last()" extension methods
Analyzers.Description: Both the Enumerable.First extension method and the LinkedList<T>.First property can be used to find the first value in a LinkedList<T>. However, LinkedList<T>.First is much faster than Enumerable.First. For small collections, the performance difference may be minor, but for large collections, it can be noticeable. The same applies for the Last property as well.

Analyzers.Title: "Contains" should be used instead of "Any" for simple equality checks
Analyzers.Description: When testing if a collection contains a specific item by simple equality, both ICollection.Contains(T item) and IEnumerable.Any(x ⇒ x == item) can be used. However, Any searches the data structure in a linear manner using a foreach loop, whereas Contains is considerably faster in some collection types, because of the underlying implementation. Analyzers.Title: Backslash should be avoided in route templates
Analyzers.Description: Backslash characters (\) should be avoided in route templates.

Analyzers.Title: ASP.NET controller actions should not have a route template starting with "/"
Analyzers.Description: Route templates for ASP.NET controller actions, defined via a RouteAttribute or any derivation of HttpMethodAttribute, should not start with "/".

Analyzers.Title: Split parameters should start on line after declaration
Analyzers.Description: The parameters to a C# method or indexer call or declaration span across multiple lines, but the first parameter does not start on the line after the opening bracket.

Analyzers.Title: Parameters should be on same line or separate lines
Analyzers.Description: The parameters to a C# method or indexer call or declaration are not all on the same line or each on a separate line.

Analyzers.Title: Parameter should not span multiple lines
Analyzers.Description: A parameter to a C# method/indexer/attribute/array, other than the first parameter, spans across multiple lines. If the parameter is short, place the entire parameter on a single line. Otherwise, save the contents of the parameter in a temporary variable and pass the temporary variable as a parameter.

Analyzers.Title: Prefix calls correctly

Analyzers.Title: Generic type constraints should be on their own line
Analyzers.Description: Each type constraint clause for a generic type parameter should be listed on a line of code by itself.

Analyzers.Title: Put constructor initializers on their own line
Analyzers.Description: A constructor initializer, including the colon character, should be on its own line.

Analyzers.Title: Do not use default value type constructor
Analyzers.Description: When creating a new instance of a value type T, the syntax 'default(T)' is functionally equivalent to the syntax 'new T()'. To avoid confusion regarding the behavior of the resulting instance, the first form is preferred.

Analyzers.Title: Use lambda syntax
Analyzers.Description: Lambda expressions are more succinct and easier to read than anonymous methods, so they should are preferred whenever the two are functionally equivalent.

Analyzers.Title: Use readable conditions
Analyzers.Description: When a comparison is made between a variable and a literal, the variable should be placed on the left-hand-side to maximize readability.

Analyzers.Title: Do not combine fields
Analyzers.Description: Each field should be declared on its own line, in order to clearly see each field of a type and allow for proper documentation of the behavior of each field.

Analyzers.Title: Do not combine attributes
Analyzers.Description: Each attribute usage should be placed in its own set of square brackets for maximum readability.

Analyzers.Title: Attributes should not share line

Analyzers.Title: Using directives should be qualified

Analyzers.Title: Enum values should be on separate lines

Analyzers.Title: Elements should have the same indentation
Analyzers.Description: Elements at the same level in the syntax tree should have the same indentation.

Analyzers.Title: Use literal suffix notation instead of casting
Analyzers.Description: Use literal suffix notation instead of casting, in order to improve readability, avoid bugs related to illegal casts and ensure that optimal IL is produced.

Analyzers.Title: Flags enums should have plural names
Analyzers.Description: A public enumeration has the System.FlagsAttribute attribute, and its name does not end in ""s"". Types that are marked by using FlagsAttribute have names that are plural because the attribute indicates that more than one value can be specified.
